 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)

You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. # Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config

- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it

Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit

  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose

   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so

   EOF
   )"

   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# ADR 0011 — Moving an issue to another project

- Status: accepted
- Date: 2026-03-18
- Supersedes: `docs/product/issue-move-notes.md` where the two disagree.

## Context

An issue filed in the wrong project has to be re-created by hand today. The product wants a
"move to project" action. Issue numbers are allocated per project and shown as `KEY-12`, the
search index and the audit log both denormalise the project an issue belongs to, and the plan
quota on issues is counted per project. This record fixes what a move means for each of them.

## Decision

1. **A move is one operation on one issue.** The issue leaves its project and joins the target
   project of the same workspace. Its title, description, status, priority, assignee, estimate,
   due date, labels, comments and attachments are untouched. Whatever the issue is linked to is
   left as it is.

2. **Numbers belong to projects.** The moved issue receives the **next number of the target
   project**, allocated exactly as a newly created issue's would be. Its old number is **retired**:
   a number that has ever been used in a project is never issued again in that project, whether
   the issue that carried it was archived, moved away, or moved away and back. Issues created in
   the source project afterwards continue after the highest number the project has ever issued.

3. **Permission.** Moving requires being allowed to edit the issue (the same permission every
   issue edit needs) **and** being allowed to create issues in the target project (the same
   permission creating one there needs). Both are checked against the acting member; a refusal
   changes nothing. The target project's per-project issue quota applies to a move exactly as it
   applies to creating an issue there, and a refused move changes nothing either.

4. **The audit log is append-only.** Entries written before the move keep the project they were
   written under. The move itself is recorded once, under the **target** project, as the action
   `issue.moved`, naming both projects and both numbers.

5. **Everything that is indexed by project follows the issue.** After a move, searching inside
   the target project finds the issue and searching inside the source project does not; the
   boards and the issue lists of both projects reflect it immediately.

6. **Announcing.** A move publishes exactly one domain event, `issue.moved`; it is not a
   creation, an edit or an archive, and publishes none of those.

## Consequences

- `KEY-12` links to the old key stop resolving; that is the cost of per-project numbering and
  is why the audit entry carries both numbers.
- The number allocator has to remember the highest number ever issued per project rather than
  derive it from the rows that happen to be in the project.

1	/**
2	 * Issue rows: the widest query surface in the app. Every method takes `orgId` first and honours `IssueFilter.includeArchived`.
3	 *
4	 * Must call (do not reimplement): archivePatch, restorePatch, shouldFilterArchived
5	 */
6	import {
7	  and,
8	  count,
9	  desc,
10	  eq,
11	  inArray,
12	  isNotNull,
13	  isNull,
14	  like,
15	  lt,
16	  or,
17	  sql,
18	} from "drizzle-orm";
19	import { newId } from "@/lib/id";
20	import {
21	  archivePatch,
22	  restorePatch,
23	  shouldFilterArchived,
24	} from "@/lib/soft-delete";
25	import { attachments, comments, getDb, issueLabels, issues } from "@/server/db";
26	import { ISSUE_STATUSES } from "@/types/issue";
27	import { toIsoTimestamp } from "@/types/common";
28	import { livePredicate, orgPredicate } from "./base-repository";
29	import { compact, keysetPredicate, probeLimit, toPage } from "./_paging";
30	import { toIssue } from "./_mappers";
31	import { listLabelsForIssues } from "./label-repository";
32	import type {
33	  CreateIssueInput,
34	  IssueFilterInput,
35	  UpdateIssueInput,
36	} from "@/schemas/issue";
37	import type {
38	  ArchiveScope,
39	  IsoTimestamp,
40	  IssueId,
41	  LabelId,
42	  OrgId,
43	  Page,
44	  ProjectId,
45	  UserId,
46	} from "@/types/common";
47	import type {
48	  Issue,
49	  IssueBoardColumn,
50	  IssueStatus,
51	  IssueWithRelations,
52	} from "@/types/issue";
53	import type { SQL } from "drizzle-orm";
54	
55	/** Statuses whose entry stamps `completed_at`; leaving one clears it again. */
56	const TERMINAL_STATUSES: readonly IssueStatus[] = ["done", "canceled"];
57	
58	export async function findIssueById(
59	  orgId: OrgId,
60	  issueId: IssueId,
61	): Promise<Issue | null> {
62	  const row = getDb()
63	    .select()
64	    .from(issues)
65	    .where(and(orgPredicate(issues.orgId, orgId), eq(issues.id, issueId)))
66	    .get();
67	  if (!row) return null;
68	
69	  const labels = await listLabelsForIssues(orgId, [row.id as IssueId]);
70	  return toIssue(row, (labels[row.id] ?? []).map((label) => label.id));
71	}
72	
73	export async function findIssueByNumber(
74	  orgId: OrgId,
75	  projectId: ProjectId,
76	  issueNumber: number,
77	): Promise<Issue | null> {
78	  const row = getDb()
79	    .select()
80	    .from(issues)
81	    .where(
82	      and(
83	        orgPredicate(issues.orgId, orgId),
84	        eq(issues.projectId, projectId),
85	        eq(issues.number, issueNumber),
86	      ),
87	    )
88	    .get();
89	  return row ? toIssue(row) : null;
90	}
91	
92	/** Builds the shared predicate list behind `listIssues` and its count. */
93	function issueFilters(input: IssueFilterInput): readonly SQL[] {
94	  const scope: ArchiveScope = shouldFilterArchived(input)
95	    ? {}
96	    : { includeArchived: true };
97	
98	  return compact(
99	    orgPredicate(issues.orgId, input.orgId),
100	    livePredicate(issues.archivedAt, scope),
101	    input.projectId === undefined
102	      ? undefined
103	      : eq(issues.projectId, input.projectId),
104	    input.status === undefined || input.status.length === 0
105	      ? undefined
106	      : inArray(issues.status, [...input.status]),
107	    input.priority === undefined || input.priority.length === 0
108	      ? undefined
109	      : inArray(issues.priority, [...input.priority]),
110	    input.assigneeId === undefined
111	      ? undefined
112	      : input.assigneeId === null
113	        ? isNull(issues.assigneeId)
114	        : eq(issues.assigneeId, input.assigneeId),
115	    input.authorId === undefined
116	      ? undefined
117	      : eq(issues.authorId, input.authorId),
118	    input.dueBefore === undefined ? undefined : lt(issues.dueAt, input.dueBefore),
119	    input.query === undefined
120	      ? undefined
121	      : or(
122	          like(issues.title, `%${input.query}%`),
123	          like(issues.description, `%${input.query}%`),
124	        ),
125	    input.labelIds === undefined || input.labelIds.length === 0
126	      ? undefined
127	      : inArray(
128	          issues.id,
129	          getDb()
130	            .select({ id: issueLabels.issueId })
131	            .from(issueLabels)
132	            .where(
133	              and(
134	                orgPredicate(issueLabels.orgId, input.orgId),
135	                inArray(issueLabels.labelId, [...input.labelIds]),
136	              ),
137	            ),
138	        ),
139	  );
140	}
141	
142	export async function listIssues(
143	  input: IssueFilterInput,
144	): Promise<Page<Issue>> {
145	  const db = getDb();
146	  const filters = issueFilters(input);
147	  const sort = { sortColumn: issues.createdAt, idColumn: issues.id };
148	
149	  const total = db
150	    .select({ value: count() })
151	    .from(issues)
152	    .where(and(...filters))
153	    .get();
154	
155	  const rows = db
156	    .select()
157	    .from(issues)
158	    .where(and(...filters, ...compact(keysetPredicate(sort, input.cursor))))
159	    .orderBy(desc(issues.createdAt), desc(issues.id))
160	    .limit(probeLimit(input.limit))
161	    .all();
162	
163	  const labels = await listLabelsForIssues(
164	    input.orgId,
165	    rows.map((row) => row.id as IssueId),
166	  );
167	
168	  return toPage(
169	    rows,
170	    input.limit,
171	    total?.value ?? 0,
172	    (row) => toIssue(row, (labels[row.id] ?? []).map((label) => label.id)),
173	    (row) => ({ id: row.id, sortValue: row.createdAt }),
174	  );
175	}

177	/**
178	 * The list view needs comment and attachment counts per row. Two grouped
179	 * queries beat N+1 round trips, so the counts are folded in afterwards.
180	 */
181	export async function listIssuesWithRelations(
182	  input: IssueFilterInput,
183	): Promise<Page<IssueWithRelations>> {
184	  const db = getDb();
185	  const page = await listIssues(input);
186	  const ids = page.items.map((issue) => issue.id);
187	  if (ids.length === 0) {
188	    return { items: [], nextCursor: page.nextCursor, total: page.total };
189	  }
190	
191	  const commentCounts = db
192	    .select({ issueId: comments.issueId, value: count() })
193	    .from(comments)
194	    .where(
195	      and(
196	        orgPredicate(comments.orgId, input.orgId),
197	        inArray(comments.issueId, [...ids]),
198	        isNull(comments.archivedAt),
199	      ),
200	    )
201	    .groupBy(comments.issueId)
202	    .all();
203	
204	  const attachmentCounts = db
205	    .select({ issueId: attachments.issueId, value: count() })
206	    .from(attachments)
207	    .where(
208	      and(
209	        orgPredicate(attachments.orgId, input.orgId),
210	        inArray(attachments.issueId, [...ids]),
211	      ),
212	    )
213	    .groupBy(attachments.issueId)
214	    .all();
215	
216	  const labels = await listLabelsForIssues(input.orgId, ids);
217	  const commentsBy = new Map(commentCounts.map((r) => [r.issueId, r.value]));
218	  const attachmentsBy = new Map(
219	    attachmentCounts.map((r) => [r.issueId, r.value]),
220	  );
221	
222	  return {
223	    items: page.items.map((issue) => ({
224	      issue,
225	      labels: labels[issue.id] ?? [],
226	      commentCount: commentsBy.get(issue.id) ?? 0,
227	      attachmentCount: attachmentsBy.get(issue.id) ?? 0,
228	    })),
229	    nextCursor: page.nextCursor,
230	    total: page.total,
231	  };
232	}

234	/** One column per status, in `ISSUE_STATUSES` order, live rows only. */
235	export async function listBoardColumns(
236	  orgId: OrgId,
237	  projectId: ProjectId,
238	): Promise<readonly IssueBoardColumn[]> {
239	  const rows = getDb()
240	    .select()
241	    .from(issues)
242	    .where(
243	      and(
244	        ...compact(
245	          orgPredicate(issues.orgId, orgId),
246	          eq(issues.projectId, projectId),
247	          livePredicate(issues.archivedAt, {}),
248	        ),
249	      ),
250	    )
251	    .orderBy(desc(issues.updatedAt))
252	    .all();
253	
254	  const labels = await listLabelsForIssues(
255	    orgId,
256	    rows.map((row) => row.id as IssueId),
257	  );
258	
259	  return ISSUE_STATUSES.map((status) => {
260	    const column = rows
261	      .filter((row) => row.status === status)
262	      .map((row) => toIssue(row, (labels[row.id] ?? []).map((l) => l.id)));
263	    return { status, issues: column, total: column.length };
264	  });
265	}

267	export async function countIssues(
268	  orgId: OrgId,
269	  projectId: ProjectId,
270	  scope: ArchiveScope = {},
271	): Promise<number> {
272	  const row = getDb()
273	    .select({ value: count() })
274	    .from(issues)
275	    .where(
276	      and(
277	        ...compact(
278	          orgPredicate(issues.orgId, orgId),
279	          eq(issues.projectId, projectId),
280	          livePredicate(issues.archivedAt, scope),
281	        ),
282	      ),
283	    )
284	    .get();
285	  return row?.value ?? 0;
286	}

288	/**
289	 * Next per-project issue number. Archived issues keep their number, so the
290	 * max is taken over every row rather than the live ones.
291	 */
292	export async function nextIssueNumber(
293	  orgId: OrgId,
294	  projectId: ProjectId,
295	): Promise<number> {
296	  const row = getDb()
297	    .select({ value: sql<number | null>`max(${issues.number})` })
298	    .from(issues)
299	    .where(
300	      and(orgPredicate(issues.orgId, orgId), eq(issues.projectId, projectId)),
301	    )
302	    .get();
303	  return (row?.value ?? 0) + 1;

/**
 * Brings `databasePath` up to date. Generated migrations win when they exist;
 * otherwise the embedded schema is pushed. Safe to run repeatedly — every
 * statement is `IF NOT EXISTS`.
 */
export async function runMigrations(
  databasePath: string = process.env.TASKFLOW_DB_PATH ?? DEFAULT_DB_PATH,
): Promise<void> {
  const absolute = resolve(process.cwd(), databasePath);
  mkdirSync(dirname(absolute), { recursive: true });

  const sqlite = new Database(absolute);
  sqlite.pragma("journal_mode = WAL");

  try {
    for (const statement of readMigrationStatements()) {
      sqlite.exec(statement);
    }
  } finally {
    sqlite.close();
  }
}

/** `pnpm db:migrate` runs this file directly; importing it must stay inert. */
if (process.argv[1]?.endsWith("migrate.ts") === true) {
  await runMigrations();
}

function readMigrationStatements(): readonly string[] {
  const dir = resolve(process.cwd(), MIGRATIONS_DIR);
  if (!existsSync(dir)) return SCHEMA_STATEMENTS;

  const files = readdirSync(dir)
    .filter((name) => name.endsWith(".sql"))
    .sort();

  if (files.length === 0) return SCHEMA_STATEMENTS;

  return files.flatMap((name) =>
    readFileSync(join(dir, name), "utf8")
      .split("--> statement-breakpoint")
      .map((chunk) => chunk.trim())
      .filter(Boolean),
  );
}
